newsitem.title: INDIA: Tear gas hangs over the road to Miss World venue.
newsitem.headline: Tear gas hangs over the road to Miss World venue.

text.p: Clouds of tear gas hung above a road leading to Chinnaswamy cricket stadium in Bangalore on Saturday after protests turned violent a few hours before the Miss World beauty pageant.
Gas canisters and stones littered the road where police repelled marchers led by local leaders of the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party.
Traffic was blocked for two hours in the centre of this south Indian city while the marchers advanced to battle police within a few hundred metres (yards) from the stadium gates.
Police also met demonstrators head-on in two other roads into the ground.
The Chinnaswamy ground in the centre of India's Garden City resembled a fortress prepared for a siege rather than the venue of a beauty pageant.
Just before midnight (1830 GMT) on Saturday one of the 88 contestants is scheduled to be crowned Miss World in front of global television audience of around two billion.

Bangalore police have drafted in more than 10,000 regular and paramilitary officers to counter militants, some of whom have threated to burn themselves to death in protest against the pageant coming to India.
Sten-gun toting troops in blue fatigues of the rapid action force, trained to tackle militant protesters, took up positions around the huge sports arena.
Jeeps with tear gas canister launchers were stationed nearby, while 150 mobile units patrolled the city's streets.
Police and paramilitary lined the route the beauty queens buses will take to the stadium from the plush hotel where they have been staying for almost two weeks.

Bomb squads with sniffer dogs have combed Chinnaswamy for unwanted packages after an unknown group calling itself the Indian Tigers exploded a couple of small devices in the weeks leading up to Saturday's finale.
Nearly 1,500 policemen and paramilitary troops will be posted in the stadium during the three-hour show, keeping a special eye out for members of a women's group who have threatened self-immolation.
Inside the stadium, stage workers putting the finishing touches to a massive set built to resemble the temples of a 14th Century south Indian Hindu empire famed for its patronage of arts and culture.
They were watched by television crews preparing for the annual event, being held in India for the first time in its 45-year history.
Aside from the parade of long-legged, glossy haired women the show will include a dance spectaculars of 480 performers and a troupe of elephants.

Around 25,000 people are expected to take their places inside the stadium an hour before the show begins just after 9.00 pm local (1530 GMT). The ground's capcity for a cricket match is 55,000. Tickets were sold at between 1,900 to 25,000 rupees ($53 to $700) apiece.
